newsitem.title: FRANCE: PARIS COURT CLEARS U.S. SCHOOL ON ENGLISH WEB SITE.
newsitem.headline: PARIS COURT CLEARS U.S. SCHOOL ON ENGLISH WEB SITE.

text.p: A Paris court on Monday sidestepped a landmark ruling on the reach of French law into cyberspace by throwing out charges that the French campus of a U.S. university illegally used only English on the Internet.

The court dismissed the complaint against the French campus of the Georgia Institute of Technology on a technicality, ruling that the two private French language watchdogs which filed the suit had failed to notify the state prosecutor's office first.

The Defence of the French Language and Future of the French Language accuse Georgia Tech Lorraine, based in Metz, eastern France. of breaking a 1994 law requiring all advertising in France be in French.

The legislation, named after former culture minister Jacques Toubon, was passed as part of a long-running battle to protect the language of Moliere and Racine against the growing global grip of English.

"The central question, the most interesting one, has not been decided today, only a procedural matter has," said Marc Jobert, lawyer for the two groups, which had demanded that the Internet site be translated into English.

While Internet champions say the worldwide web should operate free of local restraints, many national governments have asserted authority over it, often to restrict pornography or silence political dissent.
"The court did not address the underlying issue and has left us wanting more," Jacques Schaefer, lawyer for Georgia Tech, told reporters.

"It's a total victory in the sense that we were cleared of all accusations. However, when you win on a question of procedure, you're satisfied, but when you win on the substance, you're happy," he said.

Georgia Tech had argued during its hearing last January that communications on the Internet were like telephone calls. It said its website was in English because all its courses were taught in English and all its students were required to be fluent English-speakers.

Ironically, Georgia Tech Lorraine recently made its website available in French and German as well, but denies the lawsuit was the reason for this. It says technological advances in the global computer network had made it easier to provide the translation.
The two watchdog associations did not say whether they would appeal.

Mickey Mouse became the first victim of the Toubon law in March 1995 when a Paris court condemned a Disney store in Paris for failing to label about 10 types of toys with safety advice in French alongside the English stickers.
